passages.title: The Weather in the Margins
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Learning the River's Language
passages.text:
The first time I paddled the Clearwater River with my aunt Rosa, I spent most of the trip staring at the bow of my kayak. Rosa, {{1|who has guided rafting trips for twenty years}} kept telling me to look up. "The river is talking," she said. "You just have to learn {{2|it's}} language."

Over the next summer, I began to understand what she meant. Between two submerged rocks {{3|lies}} the safest channel, marked by a smooth V pointing downstream. A V pointing upstream warns of a hidden boulder. Waves that curl back on themselves, called holes, can trap a {{4|boat, even}} a skilled paddler avoids them. Reading these signs {{5|quick}} became a habit; by August I was calling out hazards before Rosa did.

{{6|Kayaks can be made of plastic, fiberglass, or wood.}} Rosa taught me to check the gauge reports each morning, because a river that rises a foot overnight {{7|can, in a very short amount of time, transform}} a gentle stretch into a dangerous one. She kept a notebook of water levels going back a decade, and she could predict, almost to the hour, when the spring melt would peak.

On my last trip of the season, Rosa let me lead. I chose our line through every rapid, and twice I steered us around holes {{8|that were near the left bank.}} {{9|Watching me pick a line through the last rapid, a grin spread across Rosa's face.}} At the take-out, she handed me her notebook. "You'll need this more than I will," she said. {{10|I still have it.}} {{11|Its pages are filled with numbers, and in every one I can hear the river talking.}}

passages.title: The Last Sign Painter in Calder
passages.genre: profile (original; Calder and Marrow are invented)
passages.text:
In the river town of Calder, nearly every storefront sign was painted by hand, and most of them {{1|was}} painted by the same woman. For forty years, Edith Marrow climbed ladders with a {{2|brush a can of enamel, and a steady hand}}, lettering the names of bakeries, barbershops, and hardware stores {{3|onto there}} windows and walls.

Marrow learned the trade from her father, who {{4|had painted signs}} for the town since before she was born. {{5|He taught her to mix colors, to space letters by eye, and that a sign should be read from across the street.}} She practiced on scrap boards in the garage, painting the alphabet hundreds of times until her strokes were {{6|identical; even}} her father could not tell them from his own.

When vinyl lettering machines arrived in the 1990s, many of Marrow's customers switched. The machines were faster and {{7|cheaper, however,}} the stickers they produced {{8|got kind of messed up}} within a few years. One by one, the shop owners came back. "A machine can make a letter," one barber told a reporter, "but it can't make a sign."

Today Marrow is in her seventies and no longer climbs ladders. {{9|Still, she enjoys gardening and reading in her spare time.}} {{10|Her students, many of whom are young and in their twenties,}} say they come for the craft but stay for the patience it teaches.

questions.evidence: Their logbooks, now stored in a state archive, record wind direction, wave height, and the color of the sky at dawn.
questions.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: Their logbooks now stored in a state archive,
choices.C: Their logbooks, now stored in a state archive
choices.D: Their logbooks; now stored in a state archive,

questions.explanation: The phrase "now stored in a state archive" adds extra information about the logbooks and could be removed without changing the sentence's core meaning ("Their logbooks record wind direction…"). Nonessential phrases are set off by a pair of commas, one before and one after, which is what the original does.

distractor_explanations.B: Removing the first comma leaves only one comma, so the phrase is not properly set off and the comma splits the subject from its verb.
distractor_explanations.C: Removing the closing comma leaves the nonessential phrase open, running it into the verb "record."
distractor_explanations.D: A semicolon must join two complete sentences; "Their logbooks" is not a complete sentence.

hints: Could the phrase between the commas be removed without breaking the sentence?
Nonessential information needs punctuation on both sides.

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence without the middle phrase; it still works, so the phrase needs a comma on each side.

questions.remember: Nonessential phrases take a pair of commas.

questions.evidence: To the keepers, these notes were routine.
questions.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.C: For example,

questions.explanation: The previous sentence says the notes were routine to the keepers; this sentence says they are treasures to scientists. These ideas contrast, so "However" is the logical transition.

distractor_explanations.A: "Similarly" signals that the second idea matches the first, but "routine" and "treasures" are opposites.
distractor_explanations.C: "For example" introduces an instance of the previous idea, but scientists valuing the notes is not an example of the notes being routine.
distractor_explanations.D: "Therefore" signals a result, but the notes being routine does not cause scientists to value them.

hints: How does "routine" compare with "treasures"?
Pick the transition that matches that relationship.

strategy.explanation: Predict a contrast word ("but," "however") before reading the choices.

questions.remember: Name the relationship first, then choose the transition.

questions.evidence: when a graduate student digitizing old shipping records found that the keepers' entries matched storm reports from passing freighters
questions.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.C: was digitizing

questions.explanation: The clause's subject is "a graduate student" and its verb is "found." The phrase "digitizing old shipping records" describes the student, so the participle "digitizing" is correct.

distractor_explanations.B: "digitized" turns the phrase into a second main verb ("a student digitized… found…") with no conjunction joining the two verbs.
distractor_explanations.C: "was digitizing" also creates a second verb for the same subject, leaving "found" without a connection.
distractor_explanations.D: "who digitizing" is ungrammatical; a relative clause needs a full verb ("who was digitizing").

hints: Find the subject and main verb of the clause beginning with "when."
The underlined word should describe the student, not act as a second main verb.

strategy.explanation: Each alternative adds a verb that collides with "found"; the participle keeps one main verb.

questions.remember: One clause, one main verb; modifiers use -ing or -ed forms.

questions.evidence: the logs offered something the ships could not: an unbroken record from a single place
questions.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.C: Unlike freighters,

questions.explanation: The sentence compares the logs with something else. Logs must be compared with other records, the freighters' reports, not with the ships themselves. And because the logs offered something the ships' reports could not, the comparison is a contrast ("Unlike").

distractor_explanations.A: This compares the logs with a ship, which is an illogical comparison of a record to a vessel.
distractor_explanations.C: This still compares logs with ships rather than with the ships' reports.
distractor_explanations.D: This compares the right things but says they are alike, contradicting the claim that the logs offered something the ships' reports could not.

hints: What exactly are the logs being compared with?
Should the comparison show a similarity or a difference?

strategy.explanation: Rule out choices that compare logs with ships; then choose contrast over similarity.

questions.remember: Compare like with like: records with records.

hints: What is the subject: the notes, or the activity of turning them into data?

strategy.explanation: Strip the phrase to "Turning … has proven"; an -ing activity is singular.

questions.evidence: is checked by at least two different people before its numbers are added to the database.
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively explains how the project protects the accuracy of the transcribed data?

choices.B: is uploaded to the website as a photograph.
choices.C: can be viewed by anyone with an internet connection.
choices.D: takes a volunteer about fifteen minutes to transcribe.

questions.explanation: The question asks how accuracy is protected. Having each page checked by two different people before the numbers are used is a quality check. The other choices describe access, format or time, not accuracy.

distractor_explanations.B: Uploading a photograph describes how pages are shared, not how errors are caught.
distractor_explanations.C: Public viewing is about access, not about checking the numbers.
distractor_explanations.D: Transcription time does not explain how accuracy is protected.

hints: Read the question's goal carefully: accuracy.
Which choice describes a way to catch mistakes?

strategy.explanation: The stem names the purpose; only one choice serves it.

questions.remember: Match the choice to the stated purpose.

questions.subskill: Adding a sentence: relevance and focus
questions.evidence: Turning handwritten notes into usable data has proven slow work.
questions.stem:
At the end of the third paragraph (after the underlined portion), the writer is considering adding the following sentence:
The lighthouse was built after a powerful storm wrecked more than two dozen ships nearby.
Should the writer make this addition there?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains why the lighthouse's records are valuable to scientists.
choices.B: Yes, because it tells when the keepers' logbooks begin.
choices.C: No, because it interrupts the paragraph's focus on how the handwritten logs are turned into data.
choices.D: No, because it contradicts the claim that the logs cover more than a century.

questions.explanation: The third paragraph explains the work of converting the keepers' shorthand into data. A sentence about why the lighthouse was built is off topic there, so it should not be added.

distractor_explanations.A: The sentence explains why the lighthouse was built, not why its records matter to scientists.
distractor_explanations.B: The sentence gives no date for the logbooks.
distractor_explanations.D: Nothing in the sentence contradicts the century-long record; the problem is focus, not accuracy.

hints: What is the third paragraph mainly about?
Does the new sentence support that topic?

strategy.explanation: Reread the paragraph's first sentence to identify its focus, then test the new sentence against it.

questions.remember: Add a sentence only if it supports the paragraph's focus.

questions.evidence: The keepers, who never imagined their notes would be read this way, simply wanted to keep the light burning and the ships safe.
questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?

choices.A: Kept, because it contrasts the keepers' practical purpose with the scientific value their notes later gained.
choices.B: Kept, because it explains how researchers measured when the lake froze.
choices.C: Deleted, because it repeats information given in the first paragraph.
choices.D: Deleted, because it shifts the focus from the lake to the design of the lighthouse.

questions.explanation: The sentence stresses that the keepers had a modest, practical goal. That sets up the final sentence's point that their careful habits became a gift to science, so the sentence should be kept.

distractor_explanations.B: The sentence says nothing about how freezing dates were measured.
distractor_explanations.C: The first paragraph says the notes were routine but does not describe the keepers' goals of keeping the light burning and ships safe.
distractor_explanations.D: The sentence is about the keepers' purpose, not the lighthouse's design.

hints: What does the sentence add that the paragraph would lose without it?
How does it connect to the sentence that follows?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence with the final sentence; the contrast between purpose and later value is the key.

questions.remember: Keep sentences that set up or support the conclusion.

questions.evidence: Rosa, who has guided rafting trips for twenty years kept telling me to look up.
questions.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: who, has guided rafting trips for twenty years
choices.C: who has guided, rafting trips for twenty years,
choices.D: who has guided rafting trips for twenty years,

questions.explanation: The clause "who has guided rafting trips for twenty years" adds nonessential information about Rosa. It opens with a comma after "Rosa," so it must close with a comma before the verb "kept."

distractor_explanations.A: Without the closing comma, the nonessential clause runs into the main verb "kept."
distractor_explanations.B: A comma between "who" and its verb splits the clause apart.
distractor_explanations.C: A comma between the verb "has guided" and its object "rafting trips" is incorrect.

hints: The clause about Rosa begins with a comma. What does it need at its end?
Nonessential clauses are set off on both sides.

strategy.explanation: Match the opening comma with a closing one; reject commas that split a verb from its subject or object.

questions.remember: Open a nonessential clause with a comma, close it with one too.

questions.evidence: You just have to learn it's language.
questions.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.C: its

questions.explanation: The sentence needs the possessive pronoun for the river's language, which is "its" with no apostrophe. "It's" means "it is."

distractor_explanations.A: "It's" is the contraction of "it is": "learn it is language" makes no sense.
distractor_explanations.B: "Its'" is not a word in standard English.
distractor_explanations.D: "Their" is plural, but it refers to the singular "river."

hints: Try reading the underlined word as "it is."
Possessive pronouns never use apostrophes.

strategy.explanation: Expand "it's" to "it is"; if that fails, use the possessive "its."

questions.remember: It's = it is; its = belonging to it.

questions.evidence: Between two submerged rocks lies the safest channel, marked by a smooth V pointing downstream.
questions.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.C: lay

questions.explanation: The sentence is inverted: its subject comes after the verb. The subject is "the safest channel," which is singular, so the verb is "lies" (present tense of "to lie," meaning to be located). "Rocks" is in the introductory prepositional phrase and is not the subject.

distractor_explanations.B: "Lie" agrees with "rocks," but "rocks" is inside the phrase "Between two submerged rocks"; the subject is "channel."
distractor_explanations.C: "Lay" is the past tense of "lie" (or the present of "to lay," which needs an object); the paragraph describes how the river works in the present.
distractor_explanations.D: "Are lying" is plural and does not agree with the singular subject "channel."

hints: Find the subject: what lies between the rocks?
Is the subject singular or plural?

strategy.explanation: Flip the sentence: "The safest channel lies between two submerged rocks." The singular present verb fits.

questions.remember: In inverted sentences, find the subject after the verb.

questions.evidence: can trap a boat, even a skilled paddler avoids them
questions.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.C: boat even

questions.explanation: "Waves … can trap a boat" and "even a skilled paddler avoids them" are both complete sentences. Joining them needs a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. "So" also shows the logical relationship: because holes can trap a boat, paddlers avoid them.

distractor_explanations.A: A comma alone between two complete sentences creates a comma splice.
distractor_explanations.C: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two sentences run together.
distractor_explanations.D: A comma after "and" incorrectly separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

hints: Are the parts before and after the comma each complete sentences?
What connects two complete sentences with a comma?

strategy.explanation: Two independent clauses need a comma + FANBOYS (or a semicolon); only B provides it correctly.

questions.remember: Comma + conjunction joins two complete sentences.

hints: Does the sentence already tell how fast the change happens?
Choose the version without repeated ideas.

strategy.explanation: All choices are grammatical; the shortest keeps the meaning without repetition.

choices.C: Rosa's face, watching me pick a line through the last rapid, grinned.
choices.D: Watching me pick a line through the last rapid, a grin was on Rosa's face.

questions.explanation: The opening phrase "Watching me pick a line through the last rapid" must describe the person doing the watching, Rosa. Only B places "Rosa" right after the phrase. In the original, the phrase seems to describe "a grin."

distractor_explanations.A: The modifier dangles: it says a grin was watching the narrator.
distractor_explanations.C: This says Rosa's face was watching and grinning, which is illogical.
distractor_explanations.D: The phrase still modifies "a grin," not Rosa.

hints: Who was watching the narrator?
That person should come right after the opening phrase.

strategy.explanation: Check the noun right after the comma in each choice; only "Rosa" can be watching.

questions.remember: An opening modifier describes the noun right after the comma.

questions.evidence: I still have it.
questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?

choices.A: Kept, because it explains why Rosa decided to give away her notebook.
choices.B: Kept, because it links the gift to the present and prepares for the final sentence about the notebook's pages.
choices.C: Deleted, because it repeats the information in the previous sentence.
choices.D: Deleted, because it shifts the focus away from the narrator's relationship with the river.

questions.explanation: "I still have it" brings the story from the past into the present and sets up the final sentence, which describes the notebook's pages now. Without it, the shift to the present tense in the last sentence would be abrupt.

distractor_explanations.A: The sentence says nothing about Rosa's reasons for giving the notebook away.
distractor_explanations.C: The previous sentence is Rosa's quotation; "I still have it" adds new information.
distractor_explanations.D: The notebook is part of the narrator's connection to the river, so the sentence keeps that focus.

hints: What would the reader lose if this sentence were removed?
How does it connect to the sentence that follows?

strategy.explanation: Read the paragraph without the sentence; the jump to the notebook's present-day pages becomes abrupt.

questions.remember: Keep sentences that bridge to what follows.

questions.evidence: "The river is talking," she said.
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively concludes the essay by connecting to its opening paragraph?

choices.B: The notebook's cover is made of faded green canvas.
choices.C: Rosa retired from guiding two years later.
choices.D: Many rivers in the region are popular with kayakers.

questions.explanation: The essay opens with Rosa saying "The river is talking." The original final sentence echoes that line: the narrator can now hear the river in the notebook's numbers. That closes the essay's arc of learning the river's language.

distractor_explanations.B: A physical description of the notebook does not connect to the opening idea.
distractor_explanations.C: Rosa's retirement is new information that does not echo the opening.
distractor_explanations.D: A general fact about the region is unrelated to the essay's personal arc.

hints: Reread the first paragraph. What memorable line does Rosa say?
Which choice echoes it?

strategy.explanation: Find the opening's key phrase, then pick the choice that returns to it.

questions.remember: Strong endings often echo the opening.

questions.evidence: Comparing the keepers' records with modern measurements, researchers have figured out that the lake now freezes
questions.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.C: figuring out

questions.explanation: The subject "researchers" is plural, so it takes "have"; the sentence also needs a complete verb for that subject. "Have figured out" provides both.

distractor_explanations.B: "Has" is singular and does not agree with the plural subject "researchers."
distractor_explanations.C: "Figuring out" is not a complete verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.
distractor_explanations.D: "To figure out" is an infinitive, which cannot serve as the sentence's main verb.

hints: What is the subject of the main clause?
Does the sentence still have a complete verb with each choice?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate the non-verbs (C, D) and the singular verb (B).

questions.remember: Plural subjects take plural verbs; every sentence needs a main verb.

choices.B: He taught her mixing colors, to space letters by eye, and that signs should be readable from across the street.
choices.C: He taught her to mix colors, to space letters by eye, and to make every sign readable from across the street.
choices.D: He taught her to mix colors, spacing letters by eye, and making every sign readable from across the street.

questions.explanation: Items in a list should share the same form. C uses three parallel infinitives: "to mix," "to space," "to make."

distractor_explanations.B: This mixes a gerund, an infinitive and a clause.
distractor_explanations.D: This mixes an infinitive with two gerunds.

hints: What form do the first two items take?
Make the third match.

strategy.explanation: Choose the version whose three items all start with "to."

questions.remember: Keep list items in the same grammatical form.

questions.evidence: The machines were faster and cheaper, however, the stickers they produced
questions.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.C: cheaper however

questions.explanation: "However" begins a new independent clause here, so it must follow a semicolon (or period) and be followed by a comma: "cheaper; however, the stickers …"

distractor_explanations.A: Commas on both sides of "however" create a comma splice between two independent clauses.
distractor_explanations.C: No punctuation fuses the clauses.
distractor_explanations.D: A single comma before "however" still splices the clauses.

hints: Are there complete sentences on both sides of "however"?
"However" is not a conjunction like "but."

strategy.explanation: Conjunctive adverb between clauses: semicolon before, comma after.

questions.remember: ; however, joins two sentences.

questions.subskill: Concluding sentence that links to earlier content
questions.evidence: She practiced on scrap boards in the garage, painting the alphabet hundreds of times
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively connects the final paragraph to the essay's description of how Marrow learned her craft?

choices.B: Still, vinyl machines remain popular in larger cities.
choices.C: Still, many of her father's signs have been painted over.
choices.D: Still, she teaches a weekend class in the old garage, where a new generation practices the alphabet on scrap boards.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes Marrow practicing the alphabet on scrap boards in the garage. D echoes that detail and shows the craft being passed on, which also sets up the next sentence about her students.

distractor_explanations.A: Gardening and reading do not connect to how she learned the craft, and they don't introduce the students mentioned next.
distractor_explanations.B: Vinyl machines relate to paragraph 3, not to how she learned.
distractor_explanations.C: Her father's signs are mentioned, but this does not connect to her training or her students.

hints: What did Marrow do in the garage when she was learning?
The next sentence mentions "Her students"; which choice introduces them?

strategy.explanation: Find the matching details in paragraph 2.

questions.remember: Good conclusions echo earlier details.

questions.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a stated goal
questions.evidence: When vinyl lettering machines arrived in the 1990s, many of Marrow's customers switched.
questions.stem: Suppose the writer's goal had been to write an essay about the history of vinyl lettering technology. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains when vinyl lettering machines first appeared.
choices.B: Yes, because it describes why shop owners stopped using vinyl stickers.
choices.C: No, because it focuses on one sign painter's craft and career, mentioning vinyl lettering only as a challenge she faced.
choices.D: No, because it never mentions vinyl lettering or any other technology.

questions.explanation: The essay is about Edith Marrow: how she learned, the challenge vinyl posed, and her teaching today. Vinyl lettering appears in one paragraph as a challenge, not as the essay's subject.

distractor_explanations.A: The essay gives one date, but one fact does not make it a history of the technology.
distractor_explanations.B: This detail serves Marrow's story; the essay does not trace the technology's development.
distractor_explanations.D: The essay does mention vinyl lettering, in paragraph 3.

hints: What is the essay mainly about?
Is vinyl lettering the subject or one detail?

strategy.explanation: Decide yes or no from the main focus, then pick the accurate reason.

questions.remember: Goal questions: compare the goal with the essay's main focus.
